doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: How to learn film scoring by watching films
summary: He advises watching films, taking notes on orchestration, and testing ideas with players; teaching orchestration is hard.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I’ve had a couple of Hamilton students who have graduated and are working on becoming a film scorer. And I wonder how do you learn to do that?

Watch a lot of films. Really. And you sort of take notes. I write everything down. If I — and you can rent them too, you don’t have to wait for it to come on television. Or now you could just download it or NetFlix. Say you want to listen to suspense music. Well spend a few weeks or months just watching suspense films from the beginning of film up and see maybe how it’s evolved or stayed the same, and then as far as how they set movies, what instruments and what instruments are doubled with other instruments, and the sonorities of sounds that these great composers got to scare you, or to make you feel that feeling of suspense. And it’s all from that. It’s hard to, you know I teach classes in orchestration at this school in Los Angeles, and it’s tough to get it from a book. That stuff you can’t get really from a book. You can learn ranges and how the instruments sound, because they have a lot of recordings of, you know, you could buy a Mozart French horn concerto and CD and listen to the French horn. You know how it sounds. But as far as understanding how to get certain sounds out of instruments coupled with other instruments to give you the sense of fear or suspense or happiness or whatever, you just have to watch films. And whatever emotions are making you feel the way you do, it’s probably going to translate that with everybody that’s watching that film. And make notes. Like have a book of suspense cues and what you’ve heard from it. And then when you have the opportunity to write some music, try it out. You could always hire musicians to read through music, because musicians always want to get together and play, and then go down to the union and just buy them lunch — buy a pizza and they’ll read through the music and then you could record that and see how it sounds, and there are many ways. But it’s a very difficult thing to teach. When I teach orchestration I don’t

say cello and clarinet is a wonderful combination for so-and-so. You have to — that’s just my point of view. And I could cite movies where that happens, but they might not like that sound. So they have to figure out for themselves what they need to do to get that sense of feeling for whatever mood they want to be put in from the movie. So you learn from all the old composers, a lot of them from the composers that I named. And that’s what I did when I was in school and when I got out of school. I would sit down and watch a movie and I would listen — oh I like that — you know, that’s a clarinet and a flute in half steps and then there’s a French horn with the ascending line to create tension. And I would write that down. And I might try that if that ever happens. You learn from the greats.
I recently watched “Twelve Years a Slave” and boy there was some really interesting music in that.
Yeah, I haven’t seen that yet.
Some of it I couldn’t even tell what is making that sound. Very, very interesting.
